# 1.1 Reading Myth: Functions, Archetypes and Xenia

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The four reasons for telling a story

Before you can analyse a single myth you need to know what a myth is *for*. The guide sets out four primary functions, and every myth in this unit can be read against them.

| Function | What the story is doing |
|---|---|
| **Metaphysical** | To teach people about a society's spiritual systems |
| **Cosmological** | To explain why the world is the way it is (before science was invented) |
| **Sociological** | To express cultural values and teach people how to be a part of their society |
| **Pedagogical** | To teach people about LIFE |

The parenthesis on the cosmological function is the important one: myth did the explanatory work that science later took over, which is why creation and origin stories dominate the early material. The sociological function is the one that matters most for the essays in this unit, because if a myth exists to "express cultural values and teach people how to be a part of their society", then the myth is evidence about the society that told it. That is the move you make every time you argue that a story reflects Greek norms.

## How women are presented in myths

The guide asks you to list and explain five main archetypes for women in myth. The one it sets out in full is the **Damsel in Distress** — the hero must rescue this vulnerable woman, and she may also be used as a trap by an evil figure to ensnare the hero. Note that the archetype has two faces: she is the reason the hero acts, and she can be the bait that gets him killed. Either way, her function in the story is defined by what she does to the hero rather than by anything of her own.

The **scapegoat** archetype is the other one the guide works through, and it is handled in full in Lesson 1.8 on Medusa.

## Patriarchy and the ideology behind the reading

The lens the unit uses is set out in one of the guide's answers: an "Ideology in which everyone could fight for gender equality," in which "People argue against patriarchy in society and culture." That is the reading position you are being taught to adopt: myths are not neutral, and the way they distribute blame, punishment and monstrosity between men and women is something you argue about rather than accept.

## Xenia and the Cyclops

**Xenia** is the central social custom in this part of the course. In ancient Greece, hospitality, or xenia, was a sacred social custom. Hosts were expected to provide travellers with food, shelter, and protection, while guests were expected to show gratitude and respect. It is a two-way obligation, and because it is sacred rather than merely polite, breaking it is an offence against the gods and not just bad manners.

When Odysseus and his men arrive at Polyphemus' cave, they expect the Cyclops to follow this norm. However, Polyphemus disregards xenia by capturing Odysseus and his men, eating some of them, and imprisoning the rest. The episode works because the audience already knows what a host owes a guest; Polyphemus is monstrous precisely by the measure of the custom he ignores.

## Penelope

Where the archetypes flatten women into functions, the text's treatment of Penelope pushes the other way. The text emphasises Penelope's intelligence and resourcefulness. It portrays her as a woman who actively engages her mind and uses her wit to navigate challenges. Penelope also expresses empathy and remorse for the hanged maids, shedding light on the injustices faced by marginalised women in the story.

That last point is the one worth holding on to for an essay: Penelope's remorse is what allows the maids' fate to register as an injustice at all. A minor character's suffering becomes visible only because a major character notices it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Metaphysical** | The function of a story that teaches people about a society's spiritual systems |
| **Cosmological** | The function of a story that explains why the world is the way it is (before science was invented) |
| **Sociological** | The function of a story that expresses cultural values and teaches people how to be a part of their society |
| **Pedagogical** | The function of a story that teaches people about LIFE |
| **Damsel in Distress** | The archetype of the vulnerable woman the hero must rescue; she may also be used as a trap by an evil figure to ensnare the hero |
| **Xenia** | Hospitality; in ancient Greece a sacred social custom under which hosts provided travellers with food, shelter and protection, while guests showed gratitude and respect |

# 1.8 Medusa

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Matching Medusa to an archetype

Medusa fits with the **scapegoat** archetype. She is the sacrificial victim because throughout the story she had done nothing wrong; it was Poseidon who raped her to get revenge on Athena. Yet in the end, Medusa is the one turned into a hideous monster.

Set the two halves of that sentence side by side and the archetype becomes obvious: the wrong is committed by one party, and the punishment lands on another. A scapegoat is not simply an unlucky character — she is the character who absorbs a punishment that belongs to someone else.

## What the myth reflects about Greek cultural norms

This story reflects ancient Greek cultural norms such as the importance of purity and virginity for women. It is evident that being a virgin is a highly regarded requirement for becoming one of Athena's priestesses. Medusa's tale also reflects the power dynamics between men and women. Even though Poseidon did the unworthy thing, at the end of the day, it was Medusa being punished.

This is the sociological function of myth doing its work. The story does not have to state that female purity matters; it encodes the value in its plot, by making the loss of virginity — even a loss inflicted by force — the thing that costs Medusa her place and her form.

## Medusa as a victim of patriarchal society

The ways in which Medusa is portrayed as a victim of patriarchy are represented in the myth when Poseidon rapes her for revenge. Medusa was threatened and raped by Poseidon in Athena's temple. Even though Poseidon assaulted Medusa, no one blamed him. Instead, Athena blamed Poseidon's actions on Medusa saying that it was because of her striking appearance that, "diverted men from the path of virtue" (49).

In this patriarchal social structure, men's disreputable actions were blamed upon women.

The quotation is the piece of evidence to memorise for this lesson, with its page reference: the blame is transferred by an argument about *her* appearance rather than *his* choice. Note also who delivers the punishment. It is Athena, a goddess, who condemns Medusa — which shows that a patriarchal structure is enforced by the women inside it as well as by the men who benefit from it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Scapegoat archetype** | The sacrificial victim — a figure who has done nothing wrong throughout the story but is punished in the end for another's actions |
| **Patriarchal social structure** | A social structure in which men's disreputable actions were blamed upon women |

# 1.9 Perseus

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The poem

> Perseus
>
> Her sleeping head with its great gelid mass of serpents torpidly astir burned into the mirroring shield-- a scathing image dire as hated truth the mind accepts at last and festers on.
> I struck.
> The shield flashed bare.
> Yet even as I lifted up the head and started from that place of gazing silences and terrored stone, I thirsted to destroy.
> None could have passed me then-- no garland-bearing girl, no priest or staring boy--and lived.

You are asked to analyse this poem and work out the narrative and events, the characterisation of Perseus, and the imagery.

## The narrative and events

The poem depicts the myth of Perseus slaying Medusa, focusing on the climactic moment when Perseus beheads her. Medusa, with her "gelid mass of serpents" representing her deadly, snake-covered head, is asleep. Perseus uses a mirroring shield to view her reflection, avoiding her petrifying gaze. He strikes her, severing her head, and immediately feels an overwhelming, violent urge to destroy more.

The narrative hints at Perseus's triumph, but also reveals the disturbing emotional transformation that accompanies his act. Notice how little of the poem is given to the kill itself — "I struck. The shield flashed bare." — and how much is given to what happens in Perseus afterwards. The proportions tell you where the poem's interest lies.

## The characterisation of Perseus

Perseus is initially characterised as a heroic figure, executing a dangerous task — killing Medusa, whose gaze turns people to stone. However, his emotions after the act reveal a more complex characterisation.

| Trait | Evidence and effect |
|---|---|
| **Determination** | Perseus successfully accomplishes a difficult task with precision and skill |
| **Violent instincts** | After beheading Medusa, Perseus experiences a shift in his emotional state. His thirst for destruction ("I thirsted to destroy") suggests that the act of killing has awakened a darker, more savage side |

The final lines extend that point: the people he imagines killing — a garland-bearing girl, a priest, a staring boy — are all harmless. The violence has stopped being aimed at a monster and become indiscriminate, which is what makes the transformation disturbing rather than heroic.

## Imagery

The images to quote are "Her sleeping head…...of serpents torpidly astir" and "gazing silences and terrored stone". This kind of imagery alludes to Medusa's hideous appearance and the tragic outcome of her victims and truly encapsulates the dire tone of the situation that Perseus is in.

## Writing it up: the PEEL paragraph

Analysis of this kind is written up in PEEL paragraphs.

| Letter | What it stands for | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| **P** | Point | Outline your main point/topic for this paragraph |
| **E** | Evidence | Support your point with evidence and examples |
| **E** | Explanation | Explain how this evidence supports your answer |
| **L** | Link | Refer this point back to the question, integrating keywords when possible or appropriate |

Could you give more than one idea while writing your PEEL paragraph? No. Absolutely not. Only include one idea in your PEEL paragraph.

That rule is what makes the Link work. If a paragraph carries a single idea, the final sentence can tie that one idea back to the question; if it carries two, there is nothing single to link.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **PEEL** | The paragraph structure: Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link — carrying only one idea per paragraph |
| **Point** | The main point or topic outlined for the paragraph |
| **Evidence** | The evidence and examples used to support your point |
| **Explanation** | The account of how this evidence supports your answer |
| **Link** | The reference back to the question, integrating keywords when possible or appropriate |

# 1.10 The Sirens' Song

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Three monsters are set out in this lesson, each described in an excerpt you are asked to read before answering the questions.

## The Sirens

> First you will come to the Sirens who enchant all who come near them. If any one unwarily draws in too close and hears the singing of the Sirens, his wife and children will never welcome him home again, for they sit in a green field and warble him to death with the sweetness of their song. There is a great heap of dead men's bones lying all around, with the flesh still rotting off them. Therefore pass these Sirens by, and stop your men's ears with wax that none of them may hear; but if you like you can listen yourself, for you may get the men to bind you as you stand upright on a cross piece half way up the mast, {99} and they must lash the rope's ends to the mast itself, that you may have the pleasure of listening. If you beg and pray the men to unloose you, then they must bind you faster.

The danger here is not force but sweetness. The wax and the ropes are needed because the victim will *want* to go, and the instruction to bind him faster if he begs assumes that his own judgement will fail at the moment it is tested.

## Scylla

> Scylla sits and yelps with a voice that you might take to be that of a young hound, but in truth she is a dreadful monster and no one-not even a god-could face her without being terror-struck. She has twelve mis-shapen feet, and six necks of the most prodigious length; and at the end of each neck she has a frightful head with three rows of teeth in each, all set very close together, so that they would crunch any one to death in a moment, and she sits deep within her shady cell thrusting out her heads and peering all round the rock, fishing for dolphins or dogfish or any larger monster that she can catch, of the thousands with which Amphitrite (Homer. 203)

## Charybdis

> "You will find the other rock lie lower, but they are so close together that there is not more than a bow-shot between them. [A large fig tree in full leaf {101} grows upon it], and under it lies the sucking whirlpool of Charybdis. Three times in the day does she vomit forth her waters, and three times she sucks them down again; see that you be not there when she is sucking, for if you are, Neptune himself could not save you; you must hug the Scylla side and drive ship by as fast as you can, for you had better lose six men than your whole crew.' (Homer, 203)

The advice at the end is worth noticing: the choice offered is not between danger and safety but between two losses, and the crew is told to accept the smaller one deliberately.

## The questions

> Would these monsters work if they were men? What would be different? Would they still represent the same fears?

The myth's portrayal of these monsters can contribute to a subconscious framing of women as dangerous or untrustworthy. The Sirens, in particular, symbolise the idea that women's beauty and allure can lead to destruction, reinforcing the stereotype that women are temptresses who lure men to their doom. Scylla's transformation into a monster may echo societal views that demonise women who exhibit anger or power, suggesting that female rage is monstrous. This might create a narrative that associates femininity with danger, perpetuating fears and mistrust.

That answer is the model for how to handle the question. Each monster is matched to the specific fear she is shaped to carry — beauty in the Sirens, rage and power in Scylla — rather than being treated as generally frightening. Read alongside Lesson 1.8, the pattern is consistent: the myth punishes or monsters the woman, and the fear being managed belongs to the men telling the story.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **The Sirens** | Monsters who enchant all who come near them and warble men to death with the sweetness of their song; they symbolise the idea that women's beauty and allure can lead to destruction |
| **Scylla** | A dreadful monster with twelve mis-shapen feet and six necks, each ending in a frightful head with three rows of teeth; her transformation may echo societal views that demonise women who exhibit anger or power |
| **Charybdis** | The sucking whirlpool that three times a day vomits forth her waters and three times sucks them down again; a ship must hug the Scylla side to pass |

# 1.11 Prometheus & Pandora

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The myth of Prometheus

You are asked to explain this myth briefly, so keep the chain of events tight.

Prometheus creates all living creatures using a combination of earth and water. Men are made in the image of the gods. Prometheus goes to Mount Olympus and enlists the help of Zeus' children. They teach him and in turn the knowledge is passed down to humanity. As punishment, Zeus prohibits the use of fire. Prometheus steals it and, as revenge, is pinned to the Caucasus.

The sequence is a sequence of transfers: knowledge moves from the gods to Prometheus, from Prometheus to humanity, and finally fire moves the same way against Zeus's express prohibition. Each transfer narrows the distance between gods and men, which is exactly what the punishment is for. Note the cosmological work being done as well — the myth explains where living creatures came from and why human beings resemble the gods.

## Pandora's Box

Myths are ingrained into culture and shape thought. With this in mind, the guide asks what ideas might be promulgated by Pandora's Box.

This myth serves as a powerful allegory for the dangers of unchecked curiosity and the unintended consequences that can arise from it. It also introduces the duality of human existence — where suffering and hope coexist — an idea that has been explored and expanded upon in countless ways in modern storytelling.

The question is phrased carefully and you should answer it in the same terms. It does not ask what the myth means; it asks what ideas the myth *promulgates* — what it teaches the culture that keeps retelling it. Because myths are ingrained into culture and shape thought, a story that ties curiosity to catastrophe is doing pedagogical work on everyone who hears it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Prometheus** | The figure who creates all living creatures from earth and water, passes the gods' knowledge down to humanity, steals fire after Zeus prohibits it, and is pinned to the Caucasus as revenge |
| **Pandora's Box** | An allegory for the dangers of unchecked curiosity and the unintended consequences that can arise from it, introducing the duality of human existence in which suffering and hope coexist |

# 2.1 Introduction to Shakespeare

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## How is Shakespeare still relevant today?

His plays are related to basic human nature, which remains constant regardless of evolutionary, industrial, or scientific developments. That is the whole argument in one line: the things the plays are about — love, ambition, grief, jealousy — are not the sorts of things that technology or scientific progress alters, so the plays do not date in the way that writing about a particular technology or a particular political arrangement would.

The second half of the answer is more concrete. Social issues we still talk about today are also central in Shakespearean plays.

| Social issue | Plays |
|---|---|
| Mental Health and Emotional Wellness | *Romeo & Juliet*, *Macbeth* |
| Racism | *Titus Andronicus*, *Othello*, *The Tempest*, *The Merchant of Venice* |

Learn the pairings rather than the general claim. An answer that says Shakespeare is relevant "because he writes about human nature" is unsupported; an answer that names the issue and the plays that carry it has evidence in it.

## Elizabethan English society

The guide leaves you with a question to work out: in Elizabethan English society, were actors, playwrights, or artists respected? Hold it against what you have just argued. The plays' survival tells you how they are valued now, which is not the same as how the people who made them were regarded at the time.

# 2.2 Shakespeare and Iambic Pentameter

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Shakespeare's writing style

Shakespeare's writing falls into three categories: **rhyming verse**, **blank verse** and **prose**. When you are asked to describe his writing style briefly, all three have to be named — an answer that mentions only verse is incomplete.

## Iambic pentameter

**Iambic pentameter** refers to ten syllables in a line of five iambs. It is a pattern of rhythm, or **meter**, in which most lines contain five unstressed syllables each followed by a stressed syllable.

The guide's example marks the five units off with bars so you can count them:

> To me | fair friend | you nev | er can | be old

Five units, two syllables each, giving the ten syllables of the definition. Say the line aloud and the pattern is audible: the second syllable of each pair carries the stress.

Note the hedge in the definition — *most* lines contain the pattern. The meter is the norm a line is measured against, not a rule every line obeys, which is why a line that breaks the pattern is worth commenting on in an analysis.

## Blank verse

His plays were written in **blank verse**, or unrhymed lines of iambic pentameter. Blank verse is therefore not a separate rhythm from iambic pentameter; it is iambic pentameter without rhyme. That is what distinguishes it from rhyming verse, the third of the categories above, which uses the same kind of line but rhymes it.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Iambic pentameter** | Ten syllables in a line of five iambs; a pattern of rhythm, or meter, in which most lines contain five unstressed syllables each followed by a stressed syllable |
| **Meter** | The pattern of rhythm in a line of verse |
| **Blank verse** | Unrhymed lines of iambic pentameter; the form Shakespeare's plays were written in |

# 3.1 Of Mice and Men

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Author: John Steinbeck.

## Setting and title

The novel is set during the Great Depression. The title comes from the poem "To a Mouse", and it reflects themes of dreams and the harshness of life: best-laid plans often fail. The title is therefore not decoration — it announces the outcome before the story starts, and every plan the characters make in the six chapters is read against it.

## The story, chapter by chapter

**Chapter 1.** George and Lennie, two migrant workers, are travelling to a new ranch in California. They stop by a river to rest for the night, revealing their close but complicated friendship. George looks after Lennie, who has a mental disability and loves to pet soft things. Lennie accidentally kills a mouse by petting it too hard, and George scolds him. Lennie dreams of tending rabbits on a farm they hope to own, while George reminds him to return to this spot if he ever gets into trouble. Both of the things that end the novel are planted here: the pattern of Lennie killing soft things by holding them too hard, and the instruction about where to go if there is trouble.

**Chapter 2.** George and Lennie arrive at the ranch, where they meet the boss, who is suspicious of Lennie's silence. They also encounter Curley, the boss's aggressive son, who immediately dislikes Lennie. Curley's flirtatious wife appears, making George wary. The old swamper Candy introduces them to other workers, including Slim, a respected mule driver, and Carlson, who complains about Candy's old dog.

**Chapter 3.** Slim gives Lennie a puppy, and George opens up to him about their past, including how Lennie got them in trouble in Weed by grabbing a woman's dress. Meanwhile, Carlson complains about Candy's old, sick dog, arguing that it would be more merciful to put it down. Candy reluctantly agrees, and Carlson takes the dog outside and shoots it, symbolising the harsh reality of the world and leaving the bunkhouse in uneasy silence. Candy overhears George and Lennie discussing their dream farm and offers his life savings to help make it a reality. Curley picks a fight with Lennie, who, after George tells him to defend himself, crushes Curley's hand.

**Chapter 4.** While most men are in town, Lennie visits Crooks, the Black stable hand, who lives alone due to segregation. Crooks initially mocks Lennie's dream but later expresses his own loneliness. Candy joins them, and for a moment, the dream farm seems possible. However, Curley's wife arrives and belittles them, reminding Crooks of his low status. After she leaves, Crooks withdraws from their dream, realising it is unlikely to happen.

**Chapter 5.** Lennie accidentally kills his puppy in the barn and is distraught. Curley's wife enters and talks about her unfulfilled dreams of being an actress. She allows Lennie to touch her soft hair, but when he grabs too hard, she panics. In his fear, Lennie accidentally breaks her neck and kills her. Realising he has done something terrible, he remembers George's instructions and flees to the river. Candy discovers the body and tells George, who understands their dream is now lost. Curley leads a mob to hunt Lennie down.

**Chapter 6.** Lennie hides by the river, imagining George scolding him and hallucinating his Aunt Clara and a giant rabbit. George arrives and, seeing no way out, tells Lennie once more about their dream farm to comfort him. As the mob closes in, George mercifully shoots Lennie in the back of the head. Slim understands George's pain and comforts him, while the other men fail to grasp the significance of what has happened.

The shooting of Candy's dog in Chapter 3 and the shooting of Lennie in Chapter 6 are built to be read together. In both, a killing is presented as a mercy, and in both the question is who should be the one to do it — Candy's regret that he let a stranger shoot his own dog is what makes George's decision at the river comprehensible.

## Themes

The guide gives five themes and adds an instruction with them: use critical thinking to find out *why* these are themes, because that is what will help you think of evidence during the ICTA or exams. Learning the label alone will not produce a paragraph; knowing which scene proves it will.

- Marginalisation / Loneliness and Isolation
- American Dream
- Life doesn't go as planned
- Friendship and Companionship
- Powerful and the Weak

Crooks, Candy and Curley's wife are the obvious route into the first theme, since each is shut out of the ranch's life for a different reason — race, age and disability, and sex — and each reveals it in a scene where they are left behind while the men go to town.

## Writing about the novel

The PEEL prompt takes the form: *How does Steinbeck portray [theme in Of Mice and Men] in Of Mice and Men?*

The essay topic given is: *How does Steinbeck portray the marginalized groups in Of Mice and Men?*

Both prompts ask how Steinbeck *portrays* something, not what happens. That wording is a direction to write about the author's choices — which character he gives a scene to, what he lets them say, what he does to them — rather than to retell the plot.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **"To a Mouse"** | The poem the novel's title comes from; it reflects themes of dreams and the harshness of life — best-laid plans often fail |
| **George** | Caring, alert, protective, responsible, tempered |
| **Lennie** | Innocent, strong, big, dependent, mentally disabled |
| **Candy** | Old, lonely, disabled, kind, loyal |
| **Curley** | Aggressive, jealous, insecure, Napoleon complex |
| **Curley's wife** | Lonely, flirtatious, desperate |
| **Slim** | Calm, wise, compassionate, respected |
| **Crooks** | Isolated, intelligent, lonely |
| **Carlson** | Blunt, insensitive |
| **The boss** | Caring, authoritative, fair |

# 4.1 A Raisin in the Sun

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Author: Lorraine Hansberry. Setting: South Side of Chicago, late 1940s – early 1950s.

## Where the title comes from

The origin of the title is "Harlem" by Langston Hughes:

> "What happens to a dream deferred? Does it dry up like a raisin in the sun?"

The title takes its question from the poem and hands it to the play: every character in the Younger family is holding a dream that has been put off, and the play works through what the waiting has done to each of them.

## The situation

This play is about the Younger family, an African American family living in a small apartment. They receive a $10,000 life insurance check after Big Walter's death. Each family member has different dreams for how to use the money, and the conflict of the play is that one sum has to satisfy five people.

| Character | What they want the money for |
|---|---|
| Lena Younger (Mama) | Wants to buy a house for the family |
| Walter Lee Younger | Wants to invest in a liquor store for financial support |
| Beneatha Younger (Bennie) | Wants to use it for her medical school tuition |
| Ruth Younger | Supports Mama but worries about the family's future |
| Travis Younger | Just exists, with his dream of being a bus driver |

Note where the money comes from. It is a life insurance payment for Big Walter's death, so the family's one chance at a dream is bought with a man's working life — which is why Mama treats spending it as a moral question rather than a financial one.

## The play, act by act

**Act I, Scene I.** The Younger family lives in a cramped apartment on Chicago's South Side.

**Act I, Scene II.** The insurance check arrives, and tensions rise over how to spend it.

**Act II, Scene I.** Mama makes a down payment on a house in a white neighbourhood (Clybourne Park).

**Act II, Scene II.** The family is excited about the new house but nervous about moving into a white area. Beneatha and George argue about assimilation versus cultural pride.

**Act II, Scene III.** A white representative from Clybourne Park, Karl Lindner, offers to buy the house back to avoid "racial tensions." The family refuses.

**Act III.** The family is in despair after losing the money.

The quotation marks the guide puts around "racial tensions" are doing work: they mark it as Lindner's phrase, a polite formula for keeping a Black family out. Reproduce them when you quote him.

## Characters

Mama is Walter's mother and the matriarch of the family — religious, stubborn and caring. Walter is Ruth's husband, a wanna-be patriarch, ambitious but selfish and rude. His sister Bennie is intelligent and independent, ambitious to find "who she is". Ruth is exhausted and pregnant, thinking about an abortion, and wishes for a stable life. Travis, Walter's son, is young — just young.

Two outside figures define Beneatha's choice between the positions argued in Act II, Scene II. Asagai, her friend, is intelligent and encourages Bennie to accept African culture. George Murchison, her boyfriend, is rich and rude, and puts money above anything. They are not simply rivals for her attention; they are the two answers to the question of cultural assimilation the play keeps asking.

## Symbols

The guide names three: Mama's plant, the insurance check, and Travis. Travis is listed as both a character and a symbol, which is the point — the child is what the dreams are ultimately for.

## Themes

- American Dream

# 4.2 A Raisin in the Sun: Critical Vocabulary and Exam Practice

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The vocabulary the play is discussed in

These are the terms the play is analysed with, and they are worth learning as a set rather than one at a time, because several of them are defined against each other. **Gender** and **sex** form one such pair: gender is a set of ideas about behaviour that a society constructs, while sex is biological. Keeping them apart is what allows an argument about Walter's "wanna-be patriarch" behaviour or Beneatha's ambition to be an argument about expectations rather than about biology.

**Apathy** and **empathy** form a second pair, and **cultural assimilation** and **Negritude** a third — the Act II argument between Beneatha and George is precisely the clash between conforming to the majority and taking pride in African identity and heritage. **Double consciousness** names the position of being pulled both ways at once, which is why it describes the Younger family's situation better than either single term does.

The remaining terms describe the structure the family lives inside. **Jim Crow**, **segregation** and **hegemony** name the legal and social arrangements; **marginalisation** and **minority group** name what those arrangements do to people. Lindner's visit in Act II, Scene III is the moment where all of them become concrete: a neighbourhood association acting to keep a minority group out of a white area.

## Essay prompts

- How does Walter Lee Younger change throughout the play?
- Explore the role of Mama (Lena Younger) in the play. How does she affect the family and the play?

The first prompt is a character-development question, so the paragraphs need to be arranged in time — Walter at the start, Walter at the turning point, Walter at the end — rather than by trait.

## Multiple-choice practice

Work these before checking the key.

**1. What is the main reason Mama entrusts Walter with part of the insurance money?**

A. She wants him to prove himself as the head of the family
B. She no longer cares how the money is spent
C. Walter threatens to leave if he doesn't get it
D. She wants him to use it only for Beneatha's education

**2. What is significant about the Youngers' decision to move into the new house despite Lindner's offer?**

A. It proves they finally achieved financial independence
B. It shows their refusal to let fear or racism control their future
C. It demonstrates Walter's need to dominate Mr. Lindner
D. It symbolizes Beneatha's dream of becoming a doctor

**3. What does Walter's decision to reject Lindner's offer show about his character development?**

A. He has become more practical and business-minded
B. He realizes dignity and pride are more important than money
C. He no longer cares about the American Dream
D. He wants to impress George Murchison

**4. Which moment in the play marks the emotional climax (change) for Walter's character?**

A. When he first tells Mama about his business plan
B. When he finds out the money is gone
C. When he tells Lindner they will move in anyway
D. When Ruth tells him she's pregnant

**Answers: 1 A, 2 B, 3 B, 4 C.**

Questions 3 and 4 are the ones to study together, because they point at the same scene from two directions and both keys land on the confrontation with Lindner. That scene is where Walter's change is completed, which is exactly the material the first essay prompt above is asking for.

## Keywords

|---|---|
| **Negritude** | Consciousness of pride in one's African identity and heritage |
| **Gender** | Ideas about how men and women should behave; something that is socially constructed |
| **Sex** | The biological differences between men and women |
| **Cultural assimilation** | When a minority conforms to the expectations, behaviours, and culture of a majority |
| **Marginalisation** | The treatment of a group of people or a concept as less important or peripheral |
| **Apathy** | A lack of caring or feeling, generally |
| **Empathy** | Caring for others as if they were you yourself |
| **Jim Crow** | Jim Crow laws were laws designed to segregate and marginalise African Americans in post-slavery America |

| **Segregation** | The action or state of separating one people to another |
| **Vernacular** | The language or dialect spoken by common people |
| **Minority group** | A culturally, ethnically, or racially distinct group that coexists with but is subordinate to a more dominant group |
| **Double consciousness** | The struggle African Americans face to remain true to black culture while at the same time conforming to the dominant white society |

# 5.1 Analysing Graphic Novels

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## The guide template

A graphic novel has to be analysed for what it does visually as well as what it says, so the template works through seven headings. The questions given under colour show the level of attention expected under all of them:

- Look at how colour (or its absence) is used in the comic.
- Does the layout stay consistent or change? Why?
- Are there repeated images or colours? What do they mean?

Each question has a second half — *why*, *what do they mean* — and that second half is where the marks are. Noticing that a layout changes is description; explaining why it changes at that point in the story is analysis.

The seven headings are colour, panels, art style, character design, text elements, symbolism and metaphor, and narrative structure.

## The worked example

The guide demonstrates the template by comparing *The Metamorphosis* with *The Best We Can Do*, and it is worth noticing what that comparison forces you to do. *The Metamorphosis* is not a graphic novel, so each visual heading has to be answered by asking what the prose does in place of the visual technique. The template survives the transfer because the categories describe narrative effects, not just drawing.

| Heading | *The Metamorphosis* |
|---|---|
| **Colour** | Kafka's prose evokes a sombre, muted atmosphere through implicit greyscale imagery, reflecting Gregor's bleak and isolated existence |
| **Panels** | While not divided into panels, Kafka's narrative is structured through chapters and descriptive passages that control the pacing |
| **Art style** | Kafka's detailed descriptions create vivid mental images of Gregor's transformation and his surroundings |
| **Character design** | Gregor's transformation into an insect is a striking metaphor for his dehumanisation, vividly described in text |
| **Text elements** | Kafka relies on narration and dialogue to convey Gregor's internal struggles and family dynamics |
| **Symbolism and metaphor** | Gregor's metamorphosis symbolises existential alienation and the dehumanising effects of modern life |
| **Narrative structure** | Kafka presents a linear narrative arc, tracing Gregor's transformation and its consequences |

Read down the column and the same argument is being made from seven angles: isolation and dehumanisation. The colour entry finds it in the greyscale atmosphere, the character design entry in the insect body, the symbolism entry states it outright. That is what a good use of the template produces — not seven unrelated observations, but seven pieces of evidence for one reading. It also shows the equivalences the template rests on: chapters and descriptive passages do the pacing work that panels do, and narration and dialogue do the work of a comic's text elements.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Colour** | How colour, or its absence, is used in the comic, including repeated colours and what they mean |
| **Panels** | The divisions that structure the narrative and control its pacing |
| **Art style** | The manner of depiction, and the mental images it creates |
| **Character design** | How a character is drawn or described, and what that design means about them |
| **Text elements** | The narration, dialogue and other written matter that carries internal struggle and character dynamics |
| **Symbolism and metaphor** | What an image or event in the work stands for beyond itself |
| **Narrative structure** | The shape of the story's arc, for example a linear arc tracing a transformation and its consequences |

# 6.1 Rhetorical Devices

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## What the finals paper contains

| Part | Task | Marks |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Vocabulary matching | 10 |
| 2 | Grammar | 10 |
| 3 | MCQ + short answers | 20 |
| 4 | SPACECAT annotation | 10 |
| 5 | Essay | 30 |

The essay is worth more than the first three parts combined, but the vocabulary in this lesson is not confined to Part 1 — the short answers in Part 3 and the Choices section of the SPACECAT annotation both require you to name devices, so learning them properly pays three times over.

## The devices you need to know

Vocabulary is tested on rhetorical devices. These are the ones the guide says you need to know, each with the example given for it.

**Allusion** is an expression designed to call something to mind without mentioning it explicitly; an indirect or passing reference.

> "He collapsed in a fit of passion, outstretching his hands to the sky." (Biblical allusion to Jesus's crucifixion.)

The example shows what makes an allusion work: the crucifixion is never named, and the reader supplies it from the posture alone.

**Hyperbole** is exaggerated statements or claims not meant to be taken literally.

> "I'm so hungry that I could eat a horse."

**Euphemism** is a mild or indirect word or expression substituted for one considered to be too harsh or blunt when referring to something unpleasant or embarrassing.

> "He's in a better place now." (Instead of saying that someone has died.)

**Juxtaposition** is two things being seen or placed close together with contrasting effect.

> "You're hot and you're cold, you're yes and you're no, you're up and down…"

**Anecdote** is a short and interesting story relevant to the topic at hand, often an amusing event, often used to support or demonstrate some point, and may be used to make an audience laugh.

**Oxymoron** is a figure of speech in which two contradictory words are put side by side to form a phrase.

> "It is bittersweet that there is no more jumbo shrimp at the grocery store."

Note the difference between this and juxtaposition. Juxtaposition places two *things* side by side for contrast; an oxymoron puts two contradictory *words* together in a single phrase — "bittersweet", "jumbo shrimp".

**Repetition** is a device that involves intentionally using a word or phrase for effect, two or more times in a speech or written work. Two named kinds are tested.

**Anaphora** is repetition at the beginning of a sentence or clauses that follow one another.

> "I declare that someday we will reach glory! I declare that one day we will hold heaven in our hands! I declare that the day is near, the day is at hand!"

**Epistrophe** is repetition at the end of a sentence or clause.

> "And so men, I ask is this the end? This cannot be the end. If this is the end, then it will be the end on our own terms."

The pair is easy to confuse and easy to keep straight: anaphora is at the start, epistrophe is at the end.

**Parallelism** is a figure of speech in which two or more elements of a sentence (or series of sentences) have the same grammatical structure. It is worth seeing that the anaphora example is also parallel — the three sentences repeat both the opening words and the shape — which is why an answer that names the structure as well as the repetition is stronger.

**Irony** occurs when the intended meaning contrasts with the literal words (e.g., saying "What a great day!" during a storm). Verbal irony is sarcasm; situational irony involves unexpected outcomes.

**Syntax** is sentence structure — how word order, length, and complexity shape meaning. Short sentences create urgency; long ones suggest depth. For example, Hemingway's terse syntax conveys bluntness, while Dickens' winding sentences evoke richness.

Syntax is the one item on this list that is not a single identifiable phrase but a property of the whole passage, which makes it the useful thing to reach for when a question asks about a stretch of text where no obvious device appears.

| **Hyperbole** | Exaggerated statements or claims not meant to be taken literally |
| **Euphemism** | A mild or indirect word or expression substituted for one considered to be too harsh or blunt when referring to something unpleasant or embarrassing |
| **Juxtaposition** | Two things being seen or placed close together with contrasting effect |
| **Anecdote** | A short and interesting story relevant to the topic at hand, often an amusing event, often used to support or demonstrate some point, and may be used to make an audience laugh |

| **Anaphora** | Repetition at the beginning of a sentence or clauses that follow one another |

# 6.2 Subject–Verb Agreement

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Part 2 of the finals is grammar, and it is tested on subject–verb agreement. The questions give you two verb forms in brackets and you choose one, so every mark comes down to identifying the subject correctly and knowing which of the seven rules below applies to it.

## The practice items

These are the sentences the guide expects the paper to look like, graded from basic to hard.

| Level | Sentence | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic | The cat (is/are) sleeping on the couch. | is | Singular subject |
| Basic | Neither the teacher nor the students (knows/know) the answer | know | Closest noun rule |
| Medium | The team (are/is) arguing about the rules. | is | Collective noun → singular verb if acting as one unit |
| Medium | Either the books or the notebook (belong/belongs) to me. | belongs | Closest noun rule |
| Medium | Ten dollars (is/are) too much for a snack. | is | Amounts = singular |
| Medium | Physics (require/requires) strong math skills. | requires | Academic subjects = singular |
| Medium | The jury (debate/debates) the verdict. | debates | Collective noun → singular |
| Hard | The list of items (is/are) on the table. | is | "List" = subject |
| Hard | Neither she nor her brothers (enjoy/enjoys) hiking. | enjoy | Closest noun rule |
| Hard | The data (suggest/suggests) a problem. | suggest (formal) | Data is technically plural |

## The secret of getting them all right

**1. Singular vs plural.** A singular subject takes a singular verb (*is, was, has, likes*); a plural subject takes a plural verb (*are, were, have, like*). "The cat is sleeping" is singular; "My friends like soccer" is plural.

**2. Tricky singulars.** These always take singular verbs. Uncountable things — news, money, physics: "The news was bad." "Ten dollars is too much." So do *each*, *neither* and *either*: "Each student has a book." Take care with the last of these, because "Neither the teacher nor the students know the answer" is governed instead by the closest-noun rule in point 4.

**3. Collective nouns (team, jury, class).** If the group is acting as one unit, the verb is singular: "The team is winning." If the members are doing their own thing, the verb is plural, which is more common in British English: "The team are fighting." This is the only rule on the list where both answers can be defensible, so the question will signal which reading it wants — *arguing about the rules* is the group acting together, so it takes *is*.

**4. Either/or and neither/nor.** The verb agrees with the closest noun. "Either the books or the notebook belongs to me" — *notebook* is singular and it is nearest the verb. "Neither she nor her brothers enjoy hiking" — *brothers* is plural and nearest. The same sentence flips its answer if the nouns are swapped round, which is why the rule is about position rather than meaning.

**5. Ignore prepositional phrases.** The verb matches the main subject, not the extra words: "The list of items is on the table." List is the subject, not *items*; list is singular and so we use *is*. This is the trick the hard questions are built on — the words nearest the verb are deliberately the wrong number.

**6. Data and media (formal vs informal).** *Data* is technically plural (*datum* is the singular), but it is often treated as singular in informal usage. In formal settings: "The data suggest a problem." In informal settings: "The data shows/suggests a problem." In an exam, answer formally.

**7. Academic subjects and titles.** Subjects like physics, mathematics and economics are singular: "Physics requires math skills." Book and film titles are singular even if plural in form: "The Lord of the Rings is my favorite book."

Rules 5 and 4 pull in opposite directions and account for most lost marks. Under rule 5 the nearest noun is a distraction to be ignored; under rule 4 the nearest noun is the thing that decides the answer. The difference is the construction: a prepositional phrase (*of items*) never contains the subject, while an either/or or neither/nor pairing offers two genuine subjects and the closest one wins.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Collective noun** | A noun such as team, jury or class; it takes a singular verb when the group acts as one unit and a plural verb when the members are doing their own thing |
| **Closest noun rule** | With either/or and neither/nor, the verb agrees with the closest noun |
| **Prepositional phrase** | Extra words following the subject, such as *of items*, which the verb does not match — the verb matches the main subject |
| **Datum** | The singular of *data*; data is technically plural, though often treated as singular in informal usage |

# 6.3 Logical Fallacies and Short Answers

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Part 3 of the finals is multiple choice plus short answers, worth 20 marks. There is not much that can be done to prepare for the multiple choice itself, but logical fallacies are likely to appear there, and the short answers follow a fixed three-step shape that can be practised.

## The fallacies

**Hasty Generalization** — drawing a general conclusion based on insufficient, unrepresentative, or biased evidence. *"I met three rude New Yorkers, so all New Yorkers are rude."* A small, possibly unrepresentative sample can't justify a broad claim about an entire group.

**Red Herring** — introducing an irrelevant topic to divert attention from the original argument (emotionally charged distractions). When discussing *"Should we raise the minimum wage?"*, someone says, *"But small businesses are struggling to survive."* The struggle of small businesses may not directly relate to the minimum wage debate, shifting focus away from the core issue.

**Slippery Slope** — arguing that a minor action will inevitably lead to extreme, negative consequences without proving this chain of events. *"If we allow teens to use social media, they'll become addicted, neglect school, and ruin their futures."* This assumes a drastic "slippery" sequence (social media → addiction → academic failure → ruined life) without evidence these steps are inevitable.

**Genetic Fallacy** — judging an idea or thing based on its origin rather than its actual merit. *"That policy is from a liberal think tank, so it must be bad."* This dismisses the policy's value by attacking its source, not analysing its content.

**Circular Argument** — using the conclusion as the premise to prove itself, so the argument goes in a circle, offering no real proof. *"The Bible is true because God wrote it, and we know God wrote it because the Bible says so."* The conclusion ("The Bible is true") relies on the premise ("God wrote it"), which relies back on the conclusion — no external evidence is used.

**Ad Populum** — claiming an idea is true or good simply because many people believe it. *"Lots of people buy this diet pill, so it must work."* Popularity doesn't equal effectiveness — many people could be wrong or misled.

**Straw Man** — misrepresenting or exaggerating an opponent's argument to make it easier to attack. Person A: *"We should limit fossil fuel use to fight climate change."* Person B: *"So you want to shut down all industries and destroy the economy? That's crazy!"* Person B distorts Person A's reasonable claim into an extreme, fictional "straw man" argument to dismiss it.

**Moral Equivalence** — equating minor moral issues with major, serious ones, creating a false sense of equal importance. *"Lying about your age online is just as bad as committing fraud."* This minimises the severity of fraud by comparing it to a trivial lie — their moral weights differ drastically.

**Either/Or (False Dilemma)** — presenting only two extreme options as the only possibilities, ignoring middle grounds or alternatives. *"Either we ban all cars, or we let pollution destroy the planet."* This ignores solutions like improving public transport, electric cars, or emissions regulations — there's more than two choices.

**Begging the Claim** — assuming the conclusion is true within the premise, so the argument "begs" the question; circular reasoning in a simpler form. *"This product is the best because it's superior to all others."* "Superior" just repeats "the best" — the premise assumes the conclusion without proof.

**Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc** — assuming that because Event B happened after Event A, A caused B, ignoring other factors. *"I wore my lucky socks, and then our team won — so the socks caused the win!"* Correlation doesn't prove causation — there could be other reasons such as team skill or opponent errors.

**Ad Hominem** — attacking a person's character, appearance, or background instead of debating their argument. *"Don't trust his tax policy — he's a dishonest person."* This dismisses the policy by attacking the person, not addressing the policy's merits.

**Non-sequitur** — a conclusion that logically doesn't follow from the premises, with no connection between the argument's parts. *"She's good at math, so she'll be a great artist."* Maths skills and artistic talent are unrelated — there's no logical link between the premise and conclusion.

Several of these are near neighbours and the paper will test the boundary between them. Circular Argument and Begging the Claim are the same error at different lengths; Genetic Fallacy and Ad Hominem both attack a source, but the genetic fallacy attacks *where an idea came from* while ad hominem attacks *the person making it*; Red Herring and Straw Man both change the subject, but the straw man distorts the opponent's own claim while the red herring introduces something else entirely.

## Practice

Name the fallacy in each.

1. My last two math teachers were terrible, so all math teachers must be bad.
2. We shouldn't worry about climate change — after all, there's still poverty and war.
3. If we allow students to redo their homework, soon they'll expect to retake every test and never take school seriously again.
4. That research comes from a conservative organization, so it can't be trusted.
5. The Bible is true because it says it's the word of God, and we know God is real because the Bible says so.
6. You shouldn't vote for her; she cheated on her boyfriend in college.
7. Everyone at school is buying this new energy drink. It must be the healthiest option.
8. You want to reduce military spending? So you want the country to be defenseless and overrun by enemies!
9. Littering is just as bad as dumping toxic waste into the ocean.
10. He got into college after buying that lucky keychain. The keychain must have helped him!

### Answers

1. **Hasty Generalization.** This person draws a broad conclusion about all math teachers based on just two examples. That's too small a sample to justify such a sweeping claim.
2. **Red Herring.** The speaker introduces a different issue (poverty and war) to distract from the original topic (climate change), diverting the conversation instead of addressing it directly.
3. **Slippery Slope.** This argument assumes that a small action (redoing homework) will inevitably lead to extreme consequences, without evidence that such a chain reaction is likely.
4. **Genetic Fallacy.** The argument attacks the origin (where the research comes from) instead of evaluating the actual quality or truth of the research itself.
5. **Circular Argument.** The claim (the Bible is true) is supported by reasoning that loops back to itself. No external evidence is provided — just circular reasoning.
6. **Ad Hominem.** This attacks the person's character instead of her qualifications or political views. Her past behaviour is unrelated to the argument at hand.
7. **Ad Populum.** Just because something is popular doesn't mean it's good or true. Popularity isn't valid evidence for effectiveness or healthiness.
8. **Straw Man.** The speaker distorts the opponent's argument into an exaggerated or extreme version (wanting no defence at all) in order to make it easier to attack.
9. **Moral Equivalence.** This compares a relatively minor wrong (littering) to a major environmental crime (dumping toxic waste), falsely suggesting they are equally serious.
10. **Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc.** This falsely assumes a cause-effect relationship just because one event followed another. There's no evidence the keychain caused the admission.

Notice that every answer names the fallacy and then says *why the reasoning fails*. A bare label is not an answer.

## Short answers

According to the English teachers, you will be given a short speech and asked short questions based on it, of the form: in this part, what is the speaker using? Why would the speaker choose that rhetoric device?

What you have to do is:

1. Identify the device
2. Explain why it's used
3. Describe the effect

Steps 2 and 3 are not the same thing, and the marks depend on separating them: *why* is about the speaker's intention, *effect* is about what happens to the audience.

**Example 1.** "Ask not what your country can do for you — ask what you can do for your country." (JFK) What device is used? Why? Effect?

> "The speaker uses antithesis (contrasting ideas)." "This highlights civic duty by flipping the perspective." "It makes the message memorable and challenges the audience to act."

Three sentences, one for each step, in order.

**Example 2.** "We are the change. We are the hope. We are the future."

> "The speaker uses anaphora (repeating 'We are'). By using anaphora the speaker builds momentum and empowers the audience to feel collective responsibility."

Here the identification quotes the repeated words themselves — *repeating 'We are'* — which is what proves the device is actually present rather than merely asserted.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Hasty Generalization** | Drawing a general conclusion based on insufficient, unrepresentative, or biased evidence |
| **Red Herring** | Introducing an irrelevant topic to divert attention from the original argument |
| **Slippery Slope** | Arguing that a minor action will inevitably lead to extreme, negative consequences without proving this chain of events |
| **Genetic Fallacy** | Judging an idea or thing based on its origin rather than its actual merit |
| **Circular Argument** | Using the conclusion as the premise to prove itself, offering no real proof |
| **Ad Populum** | Claiming an idea is true or good simply because many people believe it |
| **Straw Man** | Misrepresenting or exaggerating an opponent's argument to make it easier to attack |
| **Moral Equivalence** | Equating minor moral issues with major, serious ones, creating a false sense of equal importance |
| **Either/Or (False Dilemma)** | Presenting only two extreme options as the only possibilities, ignoring middle grounds or alternatives |
| **Begging the Claim** | Assuming the conclusion is true within the premise, so the argument "begs" the question |
| **Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc** | Assuming that because Event B happened after Event A, A caused B, ignoring other factors |
| **Ad Hominem** | Attacking a person's character, appearance, or background instead of debating their argument |
| **Non-sequitur** | A conclusion that logically doesn't follow from the premises |
| **Antithesis** | Contrasting ideas set against each other |

# 6.4 SPACECAT Annotation

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

Part 4 of the finals is a SPACECAT annotation worth 10 marks. The guide's advice on it is blunt: there is not much to say, practice makes perfect, so redo some of your SPACECAT worksheets. What follows is the checklist those worksheets run on.

## The eight letters

**S — Speaker.** Who is the speaker or writer? What do we know about them? What can you tell, or what do you know, about the speaker that helps you understand the point of view expressed?

**P — Purpose.** What is the goal of the speaker or author? The guide's examples are: support a cause, promote a change, refute a theory, stimulate interest, win an argument, arouse sympathy, provoke anger.

**A — Audience.** Who does the speaker address, and why? Do they indicate a specific audience? What assumptions exist in the text about the intended audience? If you are analysing a historical text, you are talking about the original audience or reader — not about yourself reading it now.

**C — Context.** What is the time and place of this piece? What is happening in the world as it relates to the subject of the speech or the speaker/writer?

**E — Exigence.** The circumstances surrounding the original delivery of the speech or the publication of the piece. What was the spark or catalyst that moved the speaker/writer to act or write? How did that event impact them?

Context and exigence are the pair students most often merge. Context is the general situation; exigence is the specific spark inside it that made this piece necessary *now*.

**C — Choices.** What are the rhetorical choices that the speaker or writer makes in the speech? Think about overall structure, devices, diction, syntax, and so on. This is where the vocabulary from Lesson 6.1 is spent.

**A — Appeals.** Which of the three rhetorical appeals are present in the text, and where?

**T — Tone.** The guide's entry under T repeats the appeals question rather than describing tone, so use the letter for what it stands for: the tone of the piece.

## The three appeals

| Appeal | What it is | The question to ask |
|---|---|---|
| **Ethos** | Refers to the writer's credibility and character, his or her presentation of "self"; how the writer/speaker establishes trust and respect with the audience | Is the writer/speaker ethical enough to be reliable? |
| **Pathos** | Appeals of emotion: the use of words and images to evolve emotions such as fear, anger, empathy, jealousy, pity, love | How does the speaker try to make the audience empathise with the piece? (What makes you feel?) |
| **Logos** | The use of research, facts, statistics, expert testimony, witnesses, scientific data | Does the argument make sense? Does it evoke a cognitive, rational response? |

Take care with the guide's one-line labels here: it prints "appeals of logic" beside ethos and "appeals of credibility" beside logos, but its own fuller descriptions — credibility and character for ethos, facts and statistics for logos — show that those two labels have been swapped. Go by the descriptions and the questions.

Pathos has the longest entry because it has the most ways in. It may include language that appeals to the senses, for example imagery; a bias or prejudice; an anecdote, for example a story; connotative language; figurative language; and informal language. If you can find any of those in a passage, you have found pathos, and the annotation should name which of them it is rather than simply writing "pathos" in the margin.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Speaker** | Who the speaker or writer is, and what about them helps you understand the point of view expressed |
| **Purpose** | The goal of the speaker or author — for example to support a cause, promote a change, refute a theory, stimulate interest, win an argument, arouse sympathy or provoke anger |
| **Audience** | Who the speaker addresses and why, including the assumptions the text makes about its intended audience |
| **Context** | The time and place of the piece, and what is happening in the world as it relates to its subject |
| **Exigence** | The circumstances surrounding the original delivery or publication — the spark or catalyst that moved the speaker or writer to act |
| **Choices** | The rhetorical choices the speaker or writer makes: overall structure, devices, diction, syntax and so on |
| **Appeals** | Which of the three rhetorical appeals — ethos, pathos, logos — are present in the text, and where |
| **Ethos** | The writer's credibility and character, his or her presentation of "self", and how trust and respect are established with the audience |
| **Pathos** | Appeals of emotion: the use of words and images to evolve emotions such as fear, anger, empathy, jealousy, pity and love |
| **Logos** | The use of research, facts, statistics, expert testimony, witnesses and scientific data |

# 6.5 The Essay

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

The essay is Part 5 of the finals and carries 30 marks, more than any other part of the paper. Its shape is fixed, so there is no planning decision to make under time pressure — you know before you read the passage how many paragraphs you are writing.

## The structure

One introduction, two PEEL paragraphs, one conclusion. Four paragraphs in total.

Because there are exactly two body paragraphs and each PEEL paragraph carries only one idea, the essay commits you to two ideas and no more. Choosing which two is therefore the whole of the planning: pick the two you have the strongest evidence for, not the two you thought of first.

## The introduction

Remember to add some context in the introduction. The guide's model sentence is:

> This speech was given by… To… because…

Three slots: who gave it, whom it was given to, and why. Those are the Speaker, Audience and Exigence of the SPACECAT annotation, which means the context sentence is not extra work — it is the front end of the annotation you have already been trained to do, written out as a sentence.

## The body paragraphs

Each body paragraph is a PEEL paragraph.

| Letter | What it stands for | What you do |
|---|---|---|
| **P** | Point | Outline your main point/topic for this paragraph |
| **E** | Evidence | Support your point with evidence and examples |
| **E** | Explanation | Explain how this evidence supports your answer |
| **L** | Link | Refer this point back to the question, integrating keywords when possible or appropriate |

Only include one idea in your PEEL paragraph. Not two — absolutely not. A paragraph with a second idea in it cannot be linked cleanly back to the question at the end, because there is no single thing to link.

The Link is also where the "integrating keywords" instruction earns its marks: the keywords in question are the question's own terms and the rhetorical vocabulary, so a link sentence that names the device and echoes the wording of the prompt does two jobs at once.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **PEEL** | The paragraph structure — Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link — carrying only one idea per paragraph |
| **Essay structure** | One introduction, two PEEL paragraphs and one conclusion, with context supplied in the introduction |

# 1.1 Feminist Literature, Symbols and Monsters

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Why feminist literature exists

**Feminist literature** attempts to rewrite or redefine the traditional roles of
women in literature. It exists because of the general sexism found in literature
and in society: if the inherited stock of stories gives women a narrow set of
roles, the only way to widen those roles is to write against the stock.

That purpose shapes the two methods the form uses. Feminist literature oftentimes
rewrites stories from the woman's perspective, so that a narrative already known
to readers returns with its centre of gravity moved. Alternatively it constructs
new stories in which the woman plays an important role that defies social norms
and stereotypes. Both methods answer the same problem — the first corrects an
existing text, the second supplies what the tradition never wrote.

## What symbols do for a reader

A **symbol** allows for many layers of possibilities and meanings, so that readers
can interpret the author's words independently. This is the reason writers reach
for symbols rather than statements: a stated meaning is fixed and closes the
reading down, while a symbol leaves the interpretation with the reader.

Symbols also make it easier for readers to understand and identify a central
theme. The two effects are not in conflict. The symbol points the reader towards
the theme, but leaves the layers of meaning inside that theme open.

## Rhythm and repetition in the sonnets

Both of the elements in question add a sense of rhythm and repetition to the
sonnets, and that rhythm and repetition can connect to the theme or provide
emphasis in some cases. Do not overreach when writing about them, though. Most of
the time the effect is simply that the elements help the poem flow more smoothly
and become more aesthetically pleasing to the audience, and saying so is a more
honest answer than inventing a thematic link that is not there.

## The significance of monsters in stories

Monsters often reflect or symbolise society's fears at a specific time. A monster
is therefore dated evidence: it tells you what the society that produced it was
afraid of, which is why the same figure does not recur unchanged from period to
period.

Monsters show and exaggerate the dangers of a certain thing, usually in order to
discourage or frighten people. The exaggeration is the point — the fear has to be
made visible and outsized before an audience will take the warning. Two examples
sit at either end of this pattern: *Frankenstein*, and modern movies and books
regarding artificial intelligence going wrong. Both take an anxiety about what
human beings are making and give it a body.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Feminist literature** | Literature that attempts to rewrite or redefine traditional roles of women in literature, because of the general sexism found in literature and in society |
| **Symbol** | A device that allows for many layers of possibilities and meanings, so that readers can interpret the author's words independently, and that makes it easier for readers to understand and identify a central theme |
| **Monster** | A figure that reflects or symbolises society's fears at a specific time, showing and exaggerating the dangers of a certain thing, usually to discourage or frighten people |

# 1.2 "Psyche with the Candle", "One Art" and "The Poison Tree"

> Written for SHSID from Indexademics (IDX) study guides. Original material by the IDX club; please keep this credit on any copy.

## Macleish, "Psyche with the Candle"

In the poem "Psyche with the Candle," Macleish utilises extended metaphors,
allusions to the myth of Psyche and Cupid, personification, repetition, and other
elements to convey his message. One message Macleish is suggesting could be that
the things you hold onto the tightest often end up being the things you lose.

Notice that the answer names devices and message together. The devices are not
decoration listed for their own sake; each of them is what carries the claim
about holding on too tightly. When you write on this poem, name a device and then
show it doing that work, rather than listing devices and stating the message
separately.

Note also the hedged phrasing: *one* message the poet could be suggesting. The
guide does not present this as the single correct reading, and a well-argued
alternative is available to you provided you can evidence it.

## Bishop, "One Art": the turn

The question to answer on this poem is how the turn or shift contributes to the
message Bishop is trying to articulate, and what it shows about her feelings.

Throughout the poem, Bishop uses a lighthearted tone to help convey her message,
and she repeats the phrase "it is not disaster" (or a similar phrase). That
repetition is what establishes the casual surface of the poem, and it is also
what makes the shift audible when it comes.

At the end of the poem she becomes regretful, and uses the phrase "it may seem
like disaster." The change from *is not* to *may seem like* is the whole turn: the
denial she has been repeating is withdrawn. This shows that Bishop was affected
by her experience, and that despite her casual tone, she does regret some things.

The message therefore works on two levels at once. While teaching people not to
take grief and bad times too hard, she also shares her own feelings and implies
that it is alright to be upset or regretful. An answer that reports only the
lighthearted tone misses half the poem, because it is precisely the collapse of
that tone that gives the advice its honesty.

## Blake, "The Poison Tree": a model thesis

A common task is to write a thesis with three points on the message William Blake
is trying to send in "The Poison Tree." A thesis that does the job:

> In "The Poison Tree," William Blake utilizes repetition, allusions, and an
> extended metaphor to convey the message that hiding your hatred will only make
> it grow and lead to bigger problems.

The shape of this sentence is what to copy. It names the text and the author,
lists exactly three devices, and then states a message that is a claim about the
poem rather than a summary of it. The three devices become the three body
paragraphs, and each paragraph has to end back at the same message — that
concealed hatred grows and produces bigger problems.

## Keywords

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Extended metaphor** | A metaphor sustained across a passage or a whole poem; used by Macleish in "Psyche with the Candle" and by Blake in "The Poison Tree" |
| **Allusion** | A reference to another text, story or event, such as Macleish's allusions to the myth of Psyche and Cupid |
| **Personification** | A device Macleish uses, alongside extended metaphor, allusion and repetition, to convey his message |
| **Turn (shift)** | The point at which a poem changes direction, as when Bishop moves from "it is not disaster" to "it may seem like disaster" |
| **Thesis** | A statement naming the text, the devices analysed, and the message they convey — three points for three body paragraphs |
